title: Ranat
summary: The ranat is the xylophone of Thai classical music: wooden bars strung on cords across a curved, lacquered hull that acts as the resonator, played with a mallet in each hand. Its seven steps to the octave are nearly equal.
howToPlay: Ten bars lie across the hull in order of pitch: the longest, lowest bar at the bottom.
Strike each bar as its note lands on it.
Octave pairs and quick repeated notes are the heart of the style, so listen for the rhythm of the pairs.
Start with the running figure, then try the octave doubling and the rolled repeats.
rules: The scale divides the octave into seven almost equal steps (about 171 cents each), so melodies sound unlike a European major or minor.
Ten bars cover seven steps and three more of the next octave, named 1 to 7 and 1' to 3'.
A stroke on the beat is perfect, a near one is good, and extra strokes cost points.
heritageNote: The ranat leads the melody in the Thai classical ensemble that accompanies dance-drama and shadow-play. Makers tune the bars by adding or scraping off a lump of lead and beeswax under each one.
credits: Tradition: Thai classical ranat; figures written for this game
